title: Performance of ChatGPT on USMLE: Potential for AI-assisted medical education using large language models
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT, a general-purpose large language model, can answer high-stakes medical licensing exam questions accurately enough to be useful in medical education. The central question is not whether the model was taught with a specific educational intervention, but whether its generated answers and explanations demonstrate enough correctness, internal consistency, and useful reasoning to support learners.

The authors evaluated ChatGPT on 350 publicly available USMLE sample items spanning Step 1, Step 2 CK, and Step 3. Questions were presented in three formats: open-ended prompts, multiple-choice without forced justification, and multiple-choice with forced justification. Outputs were independently adjudicated by physicians for accuracy, concordance between answer and explanation, and the presence of nonobvious but valid insights. The study was conducted using USMLE sample questions, with no human student participants; the implicit audience was medical learners, especially medical students preparing for USMLE.

Results showed that ChatGPT often performed near or above the approximate passing threshold, with accuracy varying by question format and exam step. Explanations were highly concordant with answers, and many responses contained at least one significant insight. The authors conclude that large language models may have educational value as tools that can generate reasonably accurate, interpretable, and potentially teachable explanations, though they emphasize the need for future controlled studies and better validation before real-world educational deployment.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model / chatbot that generates natural language responses from text prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated ChatGPT on USMLE sample exam questions to assess accuracy, concordance between answers and explanations, and the presence of nonobvious insights in its explanations as a proxy for medical education usefulness.

findings.finding_summary: Across 350 USMLE items, ChatGPT's accuracy varied by prompt format and exam step. With indeterminate responses censored/included, accuracy was 75.0%/45.4% for Step 1, 61.5%/54.1% for Step 2CK, and 68.8%/61.5% for Step 3 in open-ended format; 55.8%/36.1%, 59.1%/56.9%, and 61.3%/55.7% in multiple-choice no-justification format; and 64.5%/41.2%, 52.4%/49.5%, and 65.2%/59.8% in multiple-choice forced-justification format. The authors note performance approached the USMLE passing threshold (~60%) and was highest in some analyses on Steps 2CK and 3.
findings.measure: USMLE item-answer accuracy across Step 1, Step 2CK, and Step 3 under three prompt formats

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed very high answer-explanation concordance. Overall concordance was 94.6% across all questions, and concordance among accurate MC-J responses was 99.1% versus 85.1% among inaccurate responses (p<0.001).
findings.measure: Concordance between answer choice and explanation content

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT frequently produced novel, nonobvious explanations. At least one significant insight appeared in 88.9% of all responses, and mean density of insight was higher for accurate than inaccurate outputs (0.458 versus 0.199, p<0.0001). The authors argue this suggests the outputs could support human learning in medical education.
findings.measure: Presence and density of significant insights in explanations

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical performance study of ChatGPT on exam questions with physician adjudication, but it is not a randomized educational intervention or learner outcome study. The evidence is informative yet indirect for K-12 literacy use.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong model performance on a high-stakes text task and suggests potential educational usefulness, but it does not measure literacy learning gains or classroom implementation effects. The likely educational impact is therefore unclear for K-12 literacy instruction.
